description: A bunch of wannabe engineers and coders
summary:
This project began with the question: How can astronauts understand more about what is going on inside their bodies?
Living aboard the International Space Station creates several health issues that you would not face on Earth. This includes muscle and bone loss, alteration in cardiac function, sleep, and mental health. We wanted to create something that would help monitor these changes.
We created a web application called VITALIS (Vital Integrity & Telemetry Assessment for Long-duration ISS Systems). This gives astronauts the ability to monitor their health, understand how space is affecting them, identify what is concerning and what actions may be needed.
By using research from NASA’s Open Science Data Repository we have created a prototype. This shows how our application works with mock and manual data.
VITALIS gives astronauts meaningful data so they have a greater understanding of their health. This will help give astronauts peace of mind knowing what is going on in their body hundreds of km away from Earth.
details:
Project Details

VITALIS was created with the aim of helping astronauts understand their health data.

VITALIS (Vital Integrity & Telemetry Assessment for Long-duration ISS Systems) is an interactive web based platform which helps astronauts monitor and assess their health, considering the challenges they face whilst living on the International Space Station.

How VITALIS Works

VITALIS incorporates six key areas of astronaut health:

Cardiovascular

Musculoskeletal, Neurological & Visual

Immune, Behavioural Health & Sleep

Radiation & Environmental Exposure.

The astronauts input their physiological data; this can be things like heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, temperature and sleep. We also have simulated data to show how it works in our current prototype.

Once data has been inputted, it goes through a rules based assessment system to compare against example reference ranges. This helps to highlight any potential issues. Results are given in three categories: normal, attention and urgent. This includes explanations and recommendations. It is designed to help raise awareness of their health.

We also created an interactive anatomy page to help users understand how different organs and systems are impacted by microgravity. Other features include analytics, daily checklists to monitor health, informative information and an emergency simulation to show how the platform would respond to abnormal health.

What Makes Us Different?

Overall we wanted to keep VITALIS simple to understand for someone not with a medical background. We didn’t want astronauts to feel overwhelmed by complex graphs, medical terms and unrelated data.

We wanted to link their health data with explanations. Instead of just showing them an unusual cardiovascular reading, we wanted to explain why this may be an issue whilst in space flight and what they should do next.

We also wanted it to be interactive. Our anatomy page helps users visually link health risks to body parts. We also have an emergency simulation to show potentially serious situations.

Tools Used

VITALIS was created as a browser based application. We used React, JavaScript, Vite and CSS. We used SVG graphics to create our interactive anatomy page and Recharts to show health trends.

The assessment system was created using JavaScript rules. We also used LocalStorage in the browser to store example data, without needing a database or user.

We used Google Antigravity to help us and Netlify to host our application.

Our project was based around scientific research from the Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) and other NASA sources about space health.

As this is currently a software prototype there aren’t any medical sensors linked. Example and manual data is used to show how it works.

Considerations

We focussed on keeping everything accurate, simple, accessible and practical.

We considered how different body systems are affected by microgravity, how astronauts may monitor their health and how important it is to be aware of any changes.

We made sure we were clear that this is a research prototype and not a real medical device. VITALIS will not give a diagnosis and the rules used in the assessment are not NASA approved medical thresholds.

Impact & Future Development

We wanted to look into how having one simple platform can help organise, understand and be useful when monitoring astronauts health.

In the future VITALIS could be developed further to include verified wearable sensors, personal baseline health data and share relevant information securely with medical teams on earth.

As humans spend more time in space it will become increasingly important to understand and monitor their health.

VITALIS has given us a starting point to make monitoring space health more accessible, informative and personable. We wanted to create something that not only collects health data but helps people understand the story behind it.
